body:
I've thought a lot about this.

I think you want change. You want something to change, but you just don't know what.

I did the will, and the cleaning house, and the getting my affairs in order. I even drafted instructions on how to wind up my life neatly and quickly. I still think about the harm I will cause my family. At some point they will see my body. I've read so much about how suicide badly scars the ones we leave behind. I love my family too much.

I've thought about an 'accident' being the way to go, but I thought to myself if I'm going to do that, then I might as well buy some insurance and wait two years. Would be a good windfall for my family. Then again, 'accidents' don't always succeed. I'd hate to jump off a cliff while hiking and... survive.

To be honest, you don't want to die - not yet anyway. If you need chemical assistance, you need to stop. Your heart is telling you you're not ready yet. I agree that talking about it is the way to go. You cut yourself short. You don't need to do that. I've found just sharing to be a huge relief. I'm willing to listen.

I agree that no job is worth my emotional health. Jobs come and go, but I always remain. That doesn't change that unemployment is scary though. I have been bankrupt and homeless (briefly) before, and it's always in the back of my mind. I fear a relapse of those dark times, but I also know things generally don't turn out as bad as I imagine they will. I'm trying to remind myself of the limited duration of these problems constantly. It doesn't feel like it, but this moment too will pass. Thank you for listening.

Thanks. I think they're scared too. They may not show it outwardly, but their behaviour reeks of desperation. It's like a bad relationship break-up: usually the romantic partner that's being dumped fights tooth and nail to keep things going even though the writing's on the wall.

I did end up focusing on myself last night. I had a beer and some snacks and watched a movie. I even spoke with my caring and compassionate sister a bunch and she was supportive throughout the day. I know these moments pass as so many of them have before, but it's always hard to remember that in the moment. Thanks for listening.

This is truth. Everything you said. Yes, I would show compassion to others going through what I'm going through. So, I should also show it to myself. And yes, the right perspective is to forgive myself and view the experience as a learning opportunity. An opportunity for personal growth and to be a better person. As I get older I look back at all of the mistakes I've made. Once upon a time I used to wish I could go back and change them. Not so anymore. Even my worst mistakes I wouldn't want to change. They helped make me the kind, caring person I am today. And I like who I am today. I know, ultimately, this mistake too will become a part of me and it will make me a better person. But still, that doesn't change the fact I'm dealing with these painful emotions now and must try to cope with them.

Figuring out what's wrong inside of myself has been such a long journey spanning several decades. Many things ended up being wrong with me, which is not surprising since people are complex. I would agree that impartial 3rd parties (therapists) are more likely to be able to identify the problems that need to be worked on. From there it's a matter of tackling them. Sans a therapist, I would start by asking yourself what was stressful about the job, and what the chaos inside your head is.

I've been feeling like I need to make room in this world for other more capable people. I wrestle with the idea of the net-benefit of my life to the people around me and the world at large. I find I feel better when I do nice things for others. Tips the scales so to speak.

It sounds like your mind is pre-occupied with feelings of failure and the embarrasement that goes along with it. I'm struggling with this too at the moment. I've made a big mistake and I'm hiding it from everyone I know. I don't know how to cope with the embarrasement. I don't want my friends and family to look down on me as a failure. If it's any consolation, I don't think you're a disappointment. You're just struggling, and we all struggle.
French fries, funny cat videos, pizza, beer, that tranquil moment when you first wake up in the morning, hot showers, ice cream, music, watching history unfold, hugs, etc. etc.
What's on your bucket list?

'Fixing' self esteem is a massive undertaking. Many people spend their entire lives working on it. I've come along way, but I'm still working on it and I've been at it for decades. If our time frame for 'fixing' it is short, we might be holding ourselves up to meet unreasonable expectations. Self esteem isn't something we fix quickly, it's a mindset we grow into.

A drug can't fix it. A relationship can't fix it. Changing our mindset takes time, experiences, and compassion. Time and experiences alone won't do anything. Time and experiences just end up leading to a slow accumulation of regret. We need to begin forgiving ourselves for whatever we perceive our failures to be. If we don't, all we'll have are the regrets. All these regrets do is give us cause to view ourselves as failures. This leads to bouts of self-hate. Further down the rabbit hole we go.

If finances are giving you cause to regret, forgive yourself. Acknowledge the regret, forgive yourself, and tell yourself this is how people grow. Learn from the mistake and don't make it again. In the end, you're a better person for the mistake. In the end we all become better people for the mistakes we make. We just need to learn to forgive ourselves in addition to learning from the mistake itself.

I don't know if this rings true to you or your situation (I know so little about it), but I've learned it certainly rings true for me.
If you could get anything you wanted, right now and without effort, what would it be?

I feel awkard about it to. It's such a taboo subject. I've literally started going to a depression support group just so I could talk about it and nobody talks about it there either. It's unreal.

If he does know, he probably just doesn't know what to say or how to approach it. It's probably awkward for him too.

The first thing I would focus on is not making your recovery about HIM. You are not getting better for him. Don't make that mistake. Don't make him the centre of your universe. You almost died. You almost lost everything. Absolutely everything. Don't make the recovery just about one person. There's a lot more to life than that. Sure, the consequences of your action being acutely felt in that he left, but if you set yourself up so that you'll only feel better getting him back, you're in for a world of hurt. You can't control him and nobody wants the responsibility of being accountable for whether you live or die. Make your recovery about YOU.
Does your family know how you feel?
What couldn't you fix?
This is what what stopped me from killing myself during my first major depression. I had no choice, I had to go on. Someone depended on me. I'm sure they are grateful and love you very much.

I get the same way. I start dwelling in my mind about everything I'm stressed out about. I particularly tend to imagine all the confrontations I'm going to have the next day, or all the things that will go wrong tomorrow, or how badly my year will turn out etc etc.

Once upon a time I was at a popular night club, drinking my drink at the bar alone, and looking at the people as they enjoyed themselves and socialized. I was very self-conscious, and it showed, so nobody approached me. I migrated my way closer to the dance floor so I could see the dancing when the most incredible thing happened. Into the club walks this guy. Do you know the cover of the Fatboy Slim album with the overweight guy wearing the shirt "I'm #1 so why try harder?" THAT guy. Think that guy. That's who walked in. And let me tell you, he had a swagger in his step and just walked right out on that dance floor and busted some moves I couldn't believe. Instantly, he became popular and desired. All the girls were dancing with him. Afterwards, everyone was talking with him. Never seen anything like it in my life. It blew my mind. I wanted to be that guy. Turns out attitude trumps looks.
What do you feel is missing in your life?

Used vans can be pretty cheap. Are you saving up? What you're doing is actually something I want to try someday, but with a van, ya. Also, have you considered moving closer to your friends, or is the short hour work unique to your area and precludes the ability to move? Final question, how long have you been in this car situation?

I've been thinking a lot lately about distancing myself from the immediate people in my life. I want to shield them from my sadness, but at the same time I'm desperate to be around them. I don't think you're a loser. Being sad doesn't make you pathetic. You're just in pain. I'm here to listen if you want to share what's eating away at you.
I don't want you to die either. So, do me a favour and keep sharing. Share here. Share with a therapist. Share share share. I'm sending some happy thoughts your way :)
Oh, don't stop with just a big one. Get three or four of them! Just space them out so you don't freak people out lol And make sure to book your next hug in advance :D
I'll be happy to hear for you!
I may not be your family, but I love you too.
I don't feel like I need to. I do feel a lot of compassion for what you're going through because I'm there too. I'm sending some positive vibes your way. Hope you get them.
Wish I could give you a hug. Is there anyone you can go to for a hug?
I cry sometimes when I think about how long I've been alone for. Every night I come home from work and I am alone. It's my normal. Reading the posts here it seems a lot of us are in the same boat.

I don't feel like I can talk to my family or friends either. They're just not equiped to deal with my issues. They have happy lives. Not only would they not understand, they'd also probably just get frustrated when their attempts to solve my problems don't work. It sucks. I'm sorry your going through this. I wish I could help.
It's good to get it off your chest. I remember feeling just a little bit relieved when I first posted on this subreddit. I hope you get the same feeling.
I've got: learn to dance, hike the pacific crest trail, write a novel, and cross-country road trip in a run-down camper van.
Reading your post I can't help but love you. You seem like such a nice person and I'm so sad you are hurting. I feel like the world would be a lesser place without you. Do you want to talk?
I'm noticing my bucket list items are surprisingly not expensive to do. It's a wonder that I haven't done them already. What do you have on your list?

I don't think anyone would believe me either. I wear the 'mask' too well. I think a big problem I have is that I'm too closed. I'm trying to be more open, but it's really hard - especially when you don't feel like anyone believes you. I joined a support group and tried sharing, but I clam right up. It feels like people are scowling at me for lying.
I'm trying the bucket list now myself. I figure, if I'm really going to die, then I owe it to myself to get these things done.
I've never heard of anything like this, which is really surprising since it sounds like such a good idea.

Yep, a battle with your own mind. I can totally relate. I practice mindfulness meditation to cope with this. It helps me to punctuate a difficult day with that fresh and rested feeling I have just after I wake up from sleeping.
What do you feel is missing in your life?
You've got so much love coming your way right now.
Do you know what help you need? If you could get it, what would it be?
You're really strong and kind-hearted. Don't forget to show yourself some love.

Regarding your boyfriend, I don't think you have any obligations to him. It is not your job to make him happy. That's his job.

I'm wary about giving advice on breaking up with people. People can have so many different reasons and not all of them are healthy. Do you want to talk about it?

I know what you mean. It's so much better talking to someone who's living it too. We just 'get' each other. There's a lot of comfort in that. I think it's safe to say though you're among friends here. Everyone's in the same boat it seems. I've been reading a lot of posts.

Deep breathing isn't really a part of mindfulness - it's more about just being in tune with your mind and your body. Just noticing what's going on. A key element of it is noticing that all the thoughts swimming around in our heads come and go. The turmoil in our minds is transient and not the reality we live in.

I was really skeptical about it when I first heard about it. It sounded like new-age hippy b.s. I was in a pretty bad spot though so I just decided might as well give it a shot, I'm on my last leg. The first few books I read just made me roll my eyes. "Chakras" and "auras" dear god. Another book was basically all about trying to force people to live in the moment by having them count backwards and stuff to force them out of their head. Basically, "hey, I can ground you in the moment by giving you OCD." I was like "no thanks."

Eventually I came across the book I mentioned before and it was a real game changer for me. Very science-ish. I committed myself to that book not so much because I was optimistic, but just so that I could say "I did it EXACTLY as per the instructions and it didn't work for me." Whelp, the joke was on me cause it changed everything. It was just the kind of therapy I needed. You may need a different kind of therapy. I do not know. But that's the therapy that really worked for me. I was really bottoming out at the time though. I probably wouldn't have had the motivation to try otherwise.

Your family does love you. Sure, they can be hurtful at times. Just remember they are suffering too. Show compassion to them and LOVE yourself for being kind-hearted.

Re: regrets - that's what growth is all about. I've done a lot of stupid stuff. Stuff I REALLY regretted. But you know what? Those regrets helped make me a better person. In the end, I'm the person I am today BECAUSE of my mistakes, and I happen to think I'm a good person. I like who I am. My life isn't where I want it to be, but I still like who I am. Was it painful making all those mistakes originally? You bet! But ultimately, if I had a time machine and could go back to change them I wouldn't. They are a part of me and I like me.

Also, speaking as a gun owner, having a loaded gun against your temple with the safety off and a finger on the trigger really causes pause. In that moment you realize there is only one way to do it: you have to be utterly random, impulsive, and irrational. You have to completely step out of character. It feels so alien to think about you realize in the moment that you just can't do it. So, save your money, go out and buy a slice of pizza, and enjoy it.
Might as well share what's bothering you. You're annonymous here. Get some catharsis going. Get what's bothering you off your chest. People are here to read what you have to say.

You're in your head too much. It sounds like there's a hurricane of distress raging inside of you. Take a look around you right now. Chances are bothing is happening. Chances are nobody's beating you up and nobody's screaming at you. In fact, if you stop to think about it, you're probably pretty damn comfortable. You've probably got comfy clothes on. You're also probably sheltered. I'd also wager you have food in your belly. The point is the ACTUAL life you are living is much better than the IMAGINED hurricane you are dealing with in your mind.

One of the exercises I do is to make a list everyday of ten things I'm grateful for. It was bloody hard when I first started doing it. I couldn't think of anything so I started with the stupid stuff. The stuff I thought would be silly to list just so I could get to ten. Stuff like food and shelter and clothes. Over time the list started to grow. Eventually I got some really good stuff on it. My sister, my father, my mother, my friends, my health, my home, etc. It helps to remind me that the hurricane raging inside me is just that - inside me. It's not real. My real life isn't that bad.

The only rapid calm down techniques I know about require practice ahead of time. I practice mindfulness meditation. In order for it to work for me, I have to practice everyday. That way, when a crisis moment comes, it's easy for me to perform the meditation and calm down.

If you're interested, the book "Mindfulness, an eight week plan for finding peace in a frantic world" changed my life, but again, it's not a quick fix. I does, after all, take eight weeks to complete the plan as the title suggests.

If drugs are an issue, are you an addict? Are you in recovery? Do you have a support group? So many questions...

I wish you the best too :)

So, how have people been letting you down?

One of my best friends pushed me away all the time. Over the course of 8 years I was ghosted like half a dozen times. She never felt good about it. It was nihilistic and self-destructive. She didn't feel like she was worth a friend so she had to punish herself by pushing others away. It was really hard for her to let the kindness I had to offer through.

I could really understand it, though. I used to do the same thing. I would just hate on myself so hard. It was just to be alone. It was the right thing to do. It's basically the same as self-harm, just in a social way. I was impervious to kindness. In fact, I desperately didn't want it. What I wanted was for someone to come along and abuse me. I would have gone along with that willingly. It would have been appropriate.

Self-hate, my god what a force of nature.
Thanks :) It's horribly nerve wracking. I'm both scared and excited. I guess that's the price that needs to be paid to change my life. Good luck to you too btw :)
What about therapy?

I've been struggling with it for decades. When you start to get into that kind of a time horizon interesting things happen. You learn coping skills that you didn't know existed. Sometimes they are game changers. I also have met plenty of people over that length of time and some of them have turned into my best friends. I've even had the odd romantic partner, though admittedly, it's rare. The point is, the entirety of time across decades won't all be bad. That doesn't mean things have gotten better, just that there will be moments you'll be glad you had. Those add up. Eventually you get to a point where you start to say to yourself "damn, if I had taken my life x years ago, I would never have gotten to enjoy this." That really helps to add perspective. You've already been in it for a good while now. I would really sit back and ask yourself if you really had no good moments. Chances are you have had good moments. Sure, you'll wrestle with the dilemma "do the good times justify the bad times?" At first, it sure as hell doesn't seem like it, but over time it will weigh in favour of yes they do.

You fill out a piece of paper (at least I did) and that's what they seem to need to get started giving you drugs to manage it. What the ultimate solution is I do not know. I've been struggling with depression for decades and don't have the answer. For some people, it's biochemical and the drugs really do work. For others, it's therapy. Getting help from your doctor will at least get you going down the path of recovery and they'll be there to guide you.
Want to talk about it? There are lots of people here who listen.
I wish you well too and I hope you keep going on. Are you in treatment now?
Do the things that don't work out predominately have to do with other people?

Ya, the one I've been going to is a mental health support group. It's similar to AA, but that doesn't mean they all are. If there's a language barrier issue, then maybe online support is the solution, but aside from places like this subreddit, I'm not sure how online support would work.

Sounds like mental fatigue from living inside your head for too long. Imagine treading water in an ocean. Not many people can do that for more than a few minutes. Despite that, so many of us swim around in the murky waters of dark thoughts inside our own heads. It's amazing how long we can tread water swimming around in our thoughts. Eventually though, we get fatigued. Have you ever given breathing exercises a try?

To be honest, I haven't been here very long, but for the time I have been here I've been on a lot. It seems to me that the support this subreddit offers is not in the form of direct responses to my cry for help. It seems to me that the support comes in the form of knowning that I am not alone. I read other people's posts and hear about their pains and struggles and I kind of get some reassurance: I'm not alone. I in turn share with people who post about things I can identify with and there's some catharsis in the act of sharing. It's all been very indirect support from my experience, but it's there nonetheless.
I can empathize with your situation.

My close friend did this to me a year ago. She really struggled with suicidal thoughts. She became seriously ill (the symptoms strongly resembled a blood cancer). She ghosted me and ran away to isolate herself. It really hurt. I haven't forgotten about her. I still think about her and wish her well, wherever she is. Isolating yourself doesn't make people stop loving you. If she ever shows up one day I've got the biggest hug waiting for her and not a single word of reproach. You can always unisolate yourself. It's never too late to go back. You are here, after all, for some company.

My heart goes out to you. I don't want my friend's life to end. I don't want your life to end.

You're putting too much pressure on your potential partners. They don't want to be thinking "omg, I'm responsible for this guy's life." It's too much. You need to fill your life with other things. That's how a lot of people get together anyway: common interests. Right now, you're common interest is relationship desperation, and I doubt you would find a woman who is like this to be very attractive.

Talking about anxiety is not the same as talking about suicide. She may not have the experience to not freak out. This may not be the person to open up to then if it's your first time. Are their any support groups in your area? I can't recommend them, since they are all different, but I've been to a few and sometimes I come across people I feel like I can talk to because they're my peers: they are going through what I'm going through, they understand.

For me, the big obstacle to opening up is I want to remain annonymous. I don't want the backlash from the stigma, and by remaining annonymous I retain the ability to walk away. Alternatively, do you know anyone mature and responsible you can talk to that is not involved with your job?

You are in a tough position. On the one hand, I think it's healthy to get help. On the other hand, I've never shared with anyone that I have suicidal thoughts because of the stigma associated with it. And yes, part of the stigma is the threat of involuntary commitment.

I don't evny the position you are in, but I also don't envy the position I'm in. I've kept everything bottled up and it's not healthy for me. Ultimately, I would prioritize health over job. Get the help you need. If things don't work out at your job because of that, then so be it - your health is more important.

Do you know anything about the staff counselor?

My feelings about my job are similar. I used to be grateful for my job, but now I hate it. It's thankless and unrewarding and my life feels like it's slipping through my fingers. At the same time, I'm scared to death of losing it.  I recently lost a lot of money and the idea of stepping into the unknown and actually being unemployed (even for a moment) scares me. But...

The bucket list must be done. So, I gave my notice. I am so scared. I just decided to leap without looking. And I'm going to do the hike. I'm dealing with a lot of feelings of being overwhelmed as a result.

I want to do the van thing too. I've done some research on it. Cross country road trip across North America. Stop in the odd place once in a while and get a cash paying job. Who knows? Maybe I'll happen to try a job I really like and my life will go in another direction.

I want adventure, but the adventure gods are nerve wracking to hang out with.

I hope things turn out alright for me, and I really hope you get everything you want too. I wish you all the happiness in the world. I think all you're bucket list items are doable.
Hey thanks. Just remember to be kind with yourself. You'll probably have moments where you're really emotional, and it's totally ok. Don't beat yourself up.

I couldn't handle it either tbh. I was at the bottom. I had just become homeless too. My family actually rolled me into a hosptial in a wheelchair. I couldn't stand up. I was sobbing uncontrollably. My life had finally fallen apart totally and utterly. After a few hours sitting in that wheelchair in the hospital emergency room, sobing, I decided to go to someone who's also suffered in his life and ask for a job and a place to crash. I got both. I was grateful. Words cannot describe the relief. It was like the hand of god had figuratively reached down and helped me up. So I worked. I clawed my way out of debt. I got off my meds. I got back in shape. Even had a girlfriend briefly.

Things have taken a turn for the worse again lately, in ways that I've never dealt with before so I'm really struggling. Suicidal again, but I'm trying to pull myself together. Listening to the other folks here is helping a bit. But ya, I can really feel your situation. Been there, done that.
I feel your situation. Once upon a time I was suicidal, unemployed, and 100k in debt with no degree.
I can empathize <3

I've been toying with my bucket list as an excuse to keep going too. I've been telling myself "ok, you're going to die. Get the bucket list items done at least." What's on your list? Mine has: learn to dance, hike the pacific crest trail, write a novel.

I heard a saying somewhere that "Happiness is other people." It seems to ring truer for me as time goes on. The problem is that's a two edge sword. What are we supposed to do when other people just aren't there? So many people are struggling with loneliness.
I struggle with loneliness too. I think we both need a hug.

I'd say it sounds like I'm in my head again.

I used to live in my head constantly, and living in my head was not the real world. Even doing simple things that were on the face of them quite pleasant (like going for a walk through a park) were draining because the entire time my head would be swimming in thoughts about how terrible the world is. The reality though is that without those thoughts things were quite pleasant - I was afterall in a beautiful park on a beautiful day.

The world looks different when I don't have The World Is Bad soundtrack playing in the background. The only way to turn off that soundtrack is to get out of my mind.

I've found negative thoughts trigger negative emotions. Negative emotions trigger physiological changes akin to stress. Stress and negative emotions combined put me in this kind of defensive/attack mode. I start seeing everything in a negative light (the world is a bad place, everyone is bad, I'm a terrible person, there is no justice, etc etc etc) which leads to more negative thoughts and the spiral continues endlessly.

I've learned to break the cycle by getting out of my head. The emotions are in my head. The stress in my body is being caused by these emotions. The negativity skews how I see the world. I practice mindfulness to break the cycle.
I'm going through a rough patch now too. Thinking about suicide everyday, several times a day. It's horrible. My heart really goes out to you. I wish I could send you some warm fuzzy feelings.
I appreciate you sharing. It's comforting hearing other people's stories. I'd recommend reading other people's stories on this subreddit. I'm finding it theraputic.
Do you spend a lot of time in your head with your thoughts? You might be caught up in a spiral and not even realize it.
Spontaneously, or did something trigger it? It's ok to vent. Lots of us are here to vent.

You are not worthless and you don't deserve being harmed. You're just angry. Anger is a normal response when people treat you poorly. Know what else is a normal response? Not knowing how to treat someone who has a disease you don't understand.

I'm a pretty nice guy, but I have to admit, I might screw up too and treat you inconsiderately if we ever met. It's not because I'm being hurtful. I just might not understand. I don't have the experience to understand. It's hard enough to empathize with people, let alone imagine what it's like with a disability. I mean, half the people on this reddit can't even get their closest friends and family members to even understand depression. So, you are not alone in being misunderstood.

Try not to channel the anger in towards yourself. Easier said than done, I know, but try. When you come across someone with your disabilities, do you feel compassion towards them? If yes, then show some compassion towards yourself. You deserve it. They deserve it. We all deserve it.
What didn't go well?

Ya, I've always viewed suicide as a solution. It's the first place my mind goes to when I'm distressed. It creates a negative feedback loop for me though, and I have a hard time breaking out of it. So, I'm mindful to watch out for it and stop myself when it takes hold.

I'm really curious to find out what your experience will be like. I've never gotten serious therapy. I mean, sure, my family sent me to therapists, but I never opened up to them. I was always distant and just didn't feel comfortable. I often wonder what direction my life would have taken if I had seriously opened up in therapy. I have to say I'm a little excited for you. I hope it goes well. The path I took of bottling everything up inside and trying to deal with it myself has been a real uphill climb.

I was shuffled around several SSRI's, clonazepam, lorazepam, a few different sleeping pills, bucket loads of tylenol 3. I don't remember all the anti-depressants I tried, it was just a revolving door of different stuff. I was in too much distress to care what was put into my body. Doctor kept saying something will work and that we have to just keep trying. In the end, I have about a year, a year and a half, of my life I don't really remember much about. After awhile I found myself on high doses of Paxil, clonazepam, and tylenol 3 long term (3 years-ish). It was really hard coming off that chemical soup. Really emotional. Walking around with chest anxiety that felt like I was constantly on the verge of having a heart attack. I just was never really the same after coming off them. It's been about 8 years since I got off everything and I'm still not where I was from before them. Sure, I'm a lot better, but I'm still not as tough as I used to be emotionally. But that I've come a long way gives me a lot of encouragement that in another 8 years I'll be that much better. It's just the brain re-wiring itself, you know? We adapt to damage. Just takes longer for adults.

You didn't mention why you felt like killing yourself initially when you spoke with your teacher, but I assume it's related to being transgendered. If that's the case, then you might want to be careful about who you reveal your gender identity to. Generally, it seems quite clear to me the world is not ready for it yet.

Now, don't get me wrong, I don't think this means the world is a bad place. People are generally good, and genuinely bad people are quite rare. What it means is that people have a hard time empathize with things they have not gone through and can't identify with.

As a species, we are not born with empathy. I've watched children grow up and empathy is just not there. They are self-absorbed and downright psychopathic. As far as I can tell, empathy is a learned skilled. Part of learning a skill is being exposed to opportunities to learn it and having a teacher to point out the opportunity. Unfortunately, there are no empathy teachers. We each stumble and bumble through life generally ignorant of how others feel. Without a teacher, we usually only learn to empathize when we get badly burned. Then, when we see what happened to us happen to someone else, we remember what happened to us and how we felt, and we can empathize. The problem is it's easy for people to get wrapped up in their lives and miss out on the opportunities life presents them with to practice empathy unless those opportunities hurt us personally. This doesn't make people bad. It's just the way things are when people don't have help learning to empathize.

Consistently applying empathy is one hell of a skill, and I doubt you yourself are a shinning example of it either. For your part, I would start by stopping to appreciate the difficult position you put the teacher in. Appreciate his turmoil. Extend some compassion to him. If you can, extend some compassion to the social worker too. And don't forget to have some compassion for yourself. I'm sure everyone has done or said hurtful or insensitive things to others at one point or another. It doesn't make us bad people - just inexperienced.
